title: Smyrna (Revelation 2:8–11)
hook: poor but rich: be faithful unto death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephesus: a hard-working church told it had left its first love. Your line was your first love. Which first work did you do again? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

Four words in parentheses. That's the heart of today's letter. The King James Bible prints it like this: "I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich)." A poor church, under pressure, about to face worse. And in the middle of the sentence that names their poverty, almost as an aside, a correction: but you're rich. The second letter goes to the church in Smyrna. It's different from yesterday's in a way you could miss on a first read. Today we hear what's said to a church that has very little, and what isn't said.

First, who's speaking. "These things saith the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive." Of all the titles from the Patmos vision, this is the one chosen for Smyrna. To people who may face death, the one who writes has been through death and come out the other side. Second, poor but rich. Their poverty is real; the letter doesn't pretend otherwise. But it measures wealth in another currency. Jesus says something similar in the Gospels, about treasure in heaven, where moth and rust don't reach. The parentheses in the King James are small, but they turn the whole sentence. Third, what's missing. Yesterday, Ephesus got praise and then nevertheless. Smyrna gets no nevertheless. No rebuke at all. Only comfort and a warning: "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days." It doesn't promise they'll escape. Some readers hear the ten days as a limit, and the letter's "I know" tells them they won't face it unseen. Fourth, the command and the gift: "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life." Some readers note that the crown here is a victor's wreath, the kind given to someone who finishes a race, rather than a king's crown. Faithful unto death can mean faithful to the point of dying. It can also mean faithful all the way to the end of a life, one ordinary day after another. The letter closes: "He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death." The first death may come. The letter says the second will not hurt them.
screen: `THE ONE WHO WAS DEAD, AND IS ALIVE.`
`FAITHFUL UNTO DEATH: A CROWN OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay faithful in a small thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small promise you've made that nobody is checking on: a call you said you'd make, a habit you started, a person you said you'd look in on. Hold it for a moment. Notice whether it feels heavy or light. Then choose to keep it today, just today. If you pray, you can ask for help to be faithful in that one thing. If you don't, just make the choice quietly, and let your breath settle around it. The bell holds the time.
Smyrna. The poor church called rich, given no rebuke, only courage: be faithful unto death, and a crown of life.
Your line: a crown of life. Today, keep the small promise you chose, even if nobody notices, and let that be the race you finish. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Christians who face poverty or persecution read the letter to Smyrna as words addressed to them, and 'be thou faithful unto death' is read and sung in churches as words of encouragement.

original.note: Greek: a crown or wreath. the word behind 'a crown of life' in Revelation 2:10.

trapdoor: what you thought: Smyrna was a church in trouble that needed correcting.
what it means: it's the poor church called rich, with no rebuke at all: only courage, and a crown of life.
what a scholar hears: some readers note the crown is a victor's wreath, not a king's crown: a prize for finishing, not for ruling.

notes: The second half of 2:9 ('the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan') is deliberately not covered, to avoid any framing against Jews in a short lesson; a Keeper may decide whether a later day should address it carefully.
'A port city on the coast' — general geography of Smyrna; confirm acceptable.
'Ten days' read as 'the suffering has a limit' — an interpretation; confirm.
στέφανος as a victor's wreath rather than a royal crown (διάδημα): attributed to 'some readers'; confirm.
Tradition links Smyrna with Polycarp; not mentioned.
